cards.h: What keeps a star from collapsing or exploding
cards.b: A star is a balancing act. Gravity squeezes it inwards. Pressure from hot gas pushes outward. Fusion in the core supplies the heat that keeps the balance. Understanding fusion explained how the Sun has shone for billions of years, a puzzle that stumped 19th century physicists.

Lord Kelvin calculated that if the Sun were just shrinking under gravity, it could shine for only about 20 million years. But geology and fossils said Earth was far older. Chemical burning would last only thousands of years. A new energy source was needed.

In 1905 Einstein showed that mass is a form of energy: E = mc squared. A tiny bit of mass becomes a huge amount of energy because c squared is enormous. In 1920 Arthur Eddington proposed that stars convert hydrogen to helium. Four hydrogen nuclei weigh slightly more than one helium nucleus; the 0.7 percent difference is released as energy.

In the Sun, protons fuse in steps: two protons form deuterium (a proton turns into a neutron, emitting a neutrino); deuterium plus a proton makes helium-3; two helium-3 nuclei make helium-4 and release two protons. The Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second, losing about 4 million tonnes of mass as energy.

Hans Bethe worked out these steps (and the CNO cycle in heavier stars) in 1939 and won the Nobel Prize in 1967.

cards.h: Why the temperature is not enough
cards.b: Protons repel each other. Classical physics says even 15 million K is too cold for them to touch. Quantum mechanics rescues the idea: particles can tunnel through the barrier with small probability (George Gamow, 1928). The Sun's fusion is slow but there are so many protons that it works. That slowness is why the Sun lasts about 10 billion years.

cards.h: Balance, and what happens when fuel runs low
cards.b: If fusion speeds up, the core expands and cools, slowing fusion: a thermostat. When hydrogen runs out in the core, the core contracts and heats, the outer layers swell, and the star leaves the main sequence. Heavier stars go on to fuse helium to carbon and oxygen, then heavier elements up to iron, which releases no energy when fused.

Photons from the core need tens of thousands of years or more to random-walk out, but neutrinos fly straight out in 2 seconds. Raymond Davis's Homestake experiment (1960s) detected only about a third of the predicted neutrinos: the 'solar neutrino problem'. It was solved when neutrinos were shown to change type in flight (Nobel Prize 2015, Kajita and McDonald), confirming the Sun's fusion model.

• 'Stars burn like fire.' Burning needs oxygen; fusion does not.
  • 'The Sun will explode as a bomb.' It will not; its fusion is self-regulating.
  • 'Fusion is easy to copy.' On Earth it needs 100 million degrees and intense confinement.

India is a member of ITER, the international fusion experiment in France (joined 2005). The Institute for Plasma Research in Gandhinagar runs the SST-1 tokamak, India's superconducting steady-state fusion device. Scientists like Meghnad Saha (ionisation of stellar gas) and Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (stellar structure) laid foundations for this field.

• Stars shine by fusing hydrogen to helium, turning 0.7 percent of mass into energy.
  • Quantum tunnelling makes fusion possible at 15 million K.
  • Pressure from fusion balances gravity, a stable thermostat.
  • Neutrino detection confirmed solar fusion.

Think about it: (1) Why does a heavier star burn out faster? (2) Why does fusing iron not power a star?
